title: The Road Home
audience: North Indian families and a phone-first festival audience; a one-minute portrait reel explaining why Diwali is celebrated
tone: warm, clear, storybook; a grandmother answering a child, not a lecture
logline: A child asks why the whole street is lit; the answer is a city that once waited for Rama to come home, and a festival that keeps that welcome alive.

spine.want: to understand why the lamps are lit
spine.obstacle: Diwali is many stories at once, and the North Indian story is often reduced to a slogan
spine.turn: the lamps are a homecoming: Ayodhya lit the road for Rama after fourteen years
spine.button: the child lights the next diya, so the welcome continues

narration.text: Why do we light so many lamps? the child asks.
Because a whole city once waited for someone to come home.
In North India, Diwali remembers Rama's return to Ayodhya
with Sita and Lakshmana, after fourteen years of exile and his victory over Ravana.
On the darkest night of Kartik, the people cleaned their homes,
lit a diya at every door, and the road home became a river of light.
That is the heart of Diwali: light over darkness, good over evil,
and a home that keeps a lamp burning.
The festival is five days: Dhanteras, Chhoti Diwali, Lakshmi Puja,
Govardhan Puja, and Bhai Dooj, the bond of brothers and sisters.
Homes are cleaned, rangoli drawn at the door, sweets shared,
and Lakshmi welcomed with lamps and a prayer for prosperity and peace.
In the north, grain and cattle are honoured on Govardhan;
brothers and sisters mark Bhai Dooj with a tilak and a shared meal.
So the diya is not only a lamp.
It is a city remembering, a family giving, and a promise that light returns to every home.
